Family Health

Migraine around your period: symptoms and treatment choices

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Migraine attacks can cluster around a period as hormone levels change. A diary and a tailored treatment plan can help you manage that pattern. The right approach depends on attacks throughout the month, any history of aura, other health conditions and pregnancy or contraception plans.

Recognize the relationship with your period

Migraine is a neurological condition, and attacks can become more likely around menstruation. Falling estrogen levels before bleeding begins appear to contribute for some people. The relationship is usually about sensitivity to hormonal change, not simply having too much or too little of one hormone on a blood test.

The usual menstrual window runs from two days before the period starts through the first three days of bleeding. A repeated pattern across at least two of three cycles supports a menstrual relationship. Pure menstrual migraine occurs only in that window; menstrually related migraine also occurs at other times of the month.

Attacks around a period can be longer, harder to treat or more disabling than someone’s other attacks, but experiences vary. A period-related pattern is a reason to discuss a tailored plan, not a reason to accept severe pain every month. It also does not make every headache during bleeding a migraine.

Symptoms, aura and other headache types

Migraine often causes moderate or severe throbbing pain, frequently on one side, with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light or sound. Movement may make the pain worse. Bloating, breast tenderness, fatigue or mood changes can occur around the same time because of premenstrual symptoms, but they do not by themselves diagnose migraine.

Aura is a temporary neurological symptom, commonly visual zigzags, flashing lights or a changing blind area. Tingling, numbness or speech disturbance can also occur. Typical aura develops gradually and is reversible; it should not be assumed to explain new weakness, sudden loss of vision or a new speech problem. Unusual smell or taste symptoms also warrant discussion instead of being casually labeled aura.

Tension-type headache more often feels like pressure or a band, while cluster headache can cause extremely severe one-sided pain around an eye with tearing or nasal symptoms. Location alone does not distinguish them. A clinician uses the whole pattern, examination and history, including any aura even if most period-related attacks occur without it.

Keep a diary that answers useful questions

For at least two menstrual cycles, record the first day of bleeding, headache days, severity, duration, associated symptoms and any aura. Include what medicines you took and whether they helped. Tracking headaches throughout the month is important for distinguishing a purely menstrual pattern from attacks that also happen between periods.

You can also note sleep, missed meals, alcohol, caffeine changes, stress and other suspected triggers. The aim is to find a repeatable pattern, not to prove that every attack was caused by something you did. A simple calendar is enough; detailed symptom scoring is optional unless your clinician requests it.

Bring the diary and a complete medicine list to the appointment. Diagnosis is usually based on the history and examination. Blood tests, CT, MRI or lumbar puncture are considered when another cause is suspected, not routinely to prove that migraine is hormonal or to reassure everyone with a typical pattern.

Treat an attack with an agreed plan

An acute or rescue treatment is used when an attack occurs. Depending on your health and local guidance, options may include a pain reliever such as an NSAID, a triptan, a newer migraine-specific medicine or a combination. An anti-nausea medicine or a non-oral formulation may help when vomiting makes tablets difficult to keep down.

Several triptans, including rizatriptan and sumatriptan, can be used for appropriate migraine attacks. Frovatriptan is not the only approved triptan. Which medicine is licensed, and whether use for menstrual prevention is off-label, depends on the country and purpose. A clinician or pharmacist should review contraindications and interactions rather than treating the list as interchangeable choices.

Follow the agreed timing and maximum use. NSAIDs are unsuitable for some people with stomach, kidney, bleeding or pregnancy-related concerns; triptans also have important cardiovascular and other precautions. Ergot medicines have a more limited role and additional safety constraints. Calcium-channel blockers are not routine medicines to stop a migraine attack, and a water tablet is not standard treatment for menstrual migraine because of a presumed sodium problem.

Short-term prevention around a predictable period

If attacks recur predictably and acute treatment is insufficient, a clinician may suggest a short preventive course around the expected menstrual window. This is sometimes called mini-prevention. It can involve a suitable NSAID or a selected triptan such as frovatriptan, naratriptan or zolmitriptan, depending on the local plan and individual circumstances.

The start day, number of days and dose need to be agreed rather than improvised from an online example. Irregular cycles can make this strategy difficult to time. A diary helps the clinician decide whether a short course is practical or whether prevention throughout the month would fit better.

Count these treatment days together with rescue medicine used at other times. Repeated short courses are not automatically free of medication-overuse risk. Ask what to do if an attack breaks through, if bleeding starts early or if pregnancy is possible. Do not add several medicines in the same class to compensate for a late start.

When ongoing prevention is more useful

Frequent or disabling attacks throughout the month may call for a continuing preventive treatment. Options can include certain beta blockers, selected antiseizure medicines and treatments targeting calcitonin gene-related peptide, or CGRP. Botulinum toxin type A is used for selected people with chronic migraine, not simply because one attack occurs with each period.

The choice depends on headache frequency, other conditions, previous responses, side effects, cost and pregnancy plans. Some preventives are unsuitable in pregnancy and require specific precautions. Tell the prescriber if you are trying to conceive, could become pregnant or are breastfeeding before starting or changing a medicine.

Prevention is judged over an appropriate trial period using attack days, disability and rescue-medicine use, not only whether every headache disappears. Agree on a review date and ask how to change or stop treatment safely if it is ineffective or poorly tolerated. Prescription medicines should not be shared with another person who has similar symptoms.

Review contraception and hormone treatment carefully

A hormone-free interval in combined contraception can trigger attacks in some people. For an appropriate candidate, a clinician may discuss changing the formulation or schedule, or another hormonal approach. Short estrogen supplementation and continuous regimens are specialist decisions, not instructions to skip pills or add a patch on your own.

Any history of migraine with aura is a major part of this conversation. CDC classifies estrogen-containing combined pills, patches and rings as unsuitable for people with migraine with aura because of stroke risk. Having attacks without aura around a period does not erase aura experienced at another time. Progestin-only or nonhormonal options may be considered according to the full health assessment.

Smoking, blood pressure, vascular history, age and other medicines also affect suitability. Menopausal hormone therapy is a different clinical situation from combined contraception and needs its own review. Seek assessment for new aura or a substantial change in headaches after starting a hormonal treatment rather than simply adjusting the dose yourself.

Supplements have limited evidence and real precautions

Riboflavin, also called vitamin B2, coenzyme Q10, magnesium and feverfew have been studied for migraine prevention. The amount and quality of evidence vary, and benefit for migraine in general does not automatically establish benefit specifically around menstruation. Small menstrual-migraine studies exist for magnesium, so it is also too broad to say that none of these approaches has ever been studied in this context.

Ask a clinician or pharmacist about the product, dose and interactions before starting. Magnesium doses used for migraine can exceed ordinary supplement limits and may cause diarrhea or other problems; kidney health and other medicines matter. Coenzyme Q10 can interact with medicines including warfarin. “Natural” does not mean suitable for every person.

Feverfew has mixed evidence and can interact with medicines or affect bleeding. It should not be taken during pregnancy because it may affect uterine contractions, and breastfeeding safety is uncertain. Supplements should not replace effective acute treatment or delay assessment of a new headache pattern.

Exercise, stress and the let-down pattern

Regular, manageable aerobic activity may help reduce migraine burden for some people. A 2019 systematic review found a modest average reduction in migraine days, with less certain findings for attack duration and intensity. It was not proof that exercise cures menstrual migraine. Start gradually, warm up and adapt activity if exertion repeatedly triggers symptoms.

Drink appropriately and eat regular meals around activity rather than assuming a high-protein meal is a required treatment. During a severe attack, rest may be more practical than exercise. A sudden severe headache brought on by exertion needs assessment rather than being dismissed as a normal exercise trigger.

Stress and changes in stress can accompany attacks. A small 2014 diary study found an association between falling perceived stress and subsequent migraine, sometimes called a let-down headache. This does not mean that relaxing is harmful or that staying stressed prevents migraine. Breathing exercises, gentle yoga, meditation or other manageable routines may support coping without making relaxation another task you must perform perfectly.

Look for personal triggers without cutting out everything

Poor or irregular sleep, missed meals or fasting, dehydration, alcohol, caffeine excess or withdrawal, fatigue, strong smells, bright light, loud noise and weather changes may be relevant. Their effect differs between people and from one occasion to another. Some cannot be controlled, and an attack is not evidence that you failed to avoid them.

Aged or cured foods, chocolate, certain fruits, artificial sweeteners and additives such as monosodium glutamate are often blamed. A universal ban on all these foods is not necessary. Record a suspected repeatable association and discuss a focused trial if useful, while maintaining adequate nutrition.

Try small, sustainable changes such as consistent sleep and meal times. Family history, age and hormonal sensitivity can influence migraine even when daily habits are good. If avoiding triggers is making life very restrictive, revisit the treatment plan rather than continually adding new rules.

Pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause can change the pattern

Migraine can change during pregnancy; some people improve, while others continue to have attacks or develop different symptoms. Hormonal shifts, nausea with reduced intake, dehydration, sleep disruption or caffeine withdrawal can contribute to headaches. A new or severe headache in pregnancy or after birth still needs assessment, even with a previous migraine diagnosis.

During perimenopause, fluctuating hormones can make attacks less predictable. This transition varies in duration, so a fixed four-year or eight-to-ten-year timetable is not useful for predicting an individual’s migraine. Some people improve after natural menopause as fluctuations settle, but persistent or new headaches need their own evaluation.

Review medicines before pregnancy and when hormonal treatment changes. Do not assume a drug that worked before pregnancy is safe to continue unchanged, or that a new headache is “just hormones.” The same person may need a different plan at different stages of life.

When to seek urgent care and reassess treatment

Call emergency services for a sudden extremely severe headache, new weakness or facial droop, difficulty speaking, sudden vision loss, confusion, a seizure or other stroke-like symptoms. Fever with a stiff neck or a severe headache after injury also needs urgent assessment. New neurological symptoms should not be self-diagnosed as aura.

Seek prompt medical advice for a substantial change in your usual pattern, aura lasting longer than an hour, an attack lasting more than 72 hours or a headache during pregnancy or soon after birth. Severe or unusual pregnancy/postpartum symptoms may require immediate maternity or emergency assessment rather than a routine migraine appointment.

Frequent use of acute medicines can itself worsen headache. Tell the clinician how many days per month you use each product, including over-the-counter and menstrual-prevention doses. If the current plan does not restore function, ask for a review of diagnosis, acute treatment and prevention. You do not have to wait until symptoms become unbearable to seek a better plan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A menstrual diary helps establish the pattern; a hormone blood test or routine scan does not diagnose menstrual migraine.

Acute treatment, short-term menstrual prevention and ongoing prevention serve different purposes and need individualized selection.

How BeMama can help

Record attack days, period dates, aura and medicine use for a practical treatment review. Choose manageable routines and avoid blaming yourself for attacks that occur despite them.

When to seek help

Sudden severe pain or new neurological symptoms requires emergency assessment. New or severe headaches in pregnancy or after birth need prompt care. Any aura history must be discussed before estrogen-containing combined contraception.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The typical window is two days before the period through the first three days of bleeding.
  • Record attacks outside that window as well as period-related ones.
  • Frovatriptan is not the only triptan, and medicine approval depends on its use and country.
  • Migraine aura changes the suitability of combined hormonal contraception.
  • Supplements, exercise and stress strategies are supports with limitations, not guaranteed cures.

Frequently asked questions

How is pure menstrual migraine different from menstrually related migraine?

Pure menstrual migraine occurs only in the menstrual window. Menstrually related migraine also causes attacks at other times of the month.

Do I need a hormone test or MRI to diagnose it?

Usually not. The pattern and examination guide diagnosis. Tests are used when another cause is suspected, not routinely to prove a hormonal link.

Is frovatriptan the only approved triptan?

No. Several triptans are used for migraine. Licensing for specific uses, including short-term menstrual prevention, varies by country.

What is mini-prevention?

It is a clinician-planned short preventive course around a predictable menstrual window. Timing, medicine choice and total use need individual review.

Can I use a combined contraceptive pill if I have aura?

CDC guidance classifies estrogen-containing combined pills, patches and rings as unsuitable with migraine aura. Discuss another option with a clinician.

Does a water tablet treat menstrual migraine?

It is not standard migraine treatment. Do not use a diuretic for a presumed sodium problem without a separate medical indication.

Are magnesium and feverfew harmless because they are supplements?

No. Doses, interactions and health conditions matter. Feverfew should not be taken during pregnancy, and migraine-dose magnesium needs clinical guidance.

Does a let-down headache mean I should stay stressed?

No. Observational research does not show that maintaining stress prevents migraine. Sustainable routines and coping support can still help.

Must I avoid every food described as a trigger?

No. Look for a repeatable personal pattern and avoid unnecessary broad restrictions. Regular meals and adequate nutrition remain important.

When should I treat a headache as an emergency?

A sudden extremely severe headache, new weakness, speech or vision loss, confusion or seizure needs emergency assessment. Do not assume new neurological symptoms are ordinary aura.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
